items.q: A 55-year-old patient diagnosed with acute pericarditis reports a persistent fever of 38.5 degrees Celsius despite one week of ibuprofen therapy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Continue current NSAID dosage alone
Hospital admission for further evaluation
Switch to corticosteroids as monotherapy
Schedule outpatient follow-up in one month
items.exp: Fever >38C and lack of response to NSAIDs after one week are high-risk features requiring admission.
r: Lack of response after one week is a high-risk feature that necessitates further clinical assessment.
Fever >38C and lack of response to NSAIDs after one week are high-risk features requiring admission.
Corticosteroids are not recommended as first-line therapy for acute pericarditis.
High-risk patients with fever and treatment failure require prompt inpatient evaluation.
items.kp: High-risk features for pericarditis include fever >38C, large effusion, tamponade, or NSAID failure.

items.q: A 62-year-old male post-MI presents with symptoms suggestive of acute pericarditis. Which pharmacological regimen is most appropriate for initial therapy?
o: High-dose aspirin and colchicine
Corticosteroids and aspirin
High-dose ibuprofen and colchicine
High-dose aspirin without colchicine
items.exp: Aspirin is preferred over NSAIDs for patients requiring antiplatelet therapy following a myocardial infarction.
r: Aspirin is preferred over NSAIDs for patients requiring antiplatelet therapy following a myocardial infarction.
Corticosteroids should be avoided as first-line therapy for acute pericarditis.
Aspirin is preferred when the patient is already on antiplatelet therapy post-MI.
Colchicine is recommended as an adjunct to reduce recurrence rates in pericarditis.
items.kp: Aspirin is preferred for pericarditis in patients requiring antiplatelet therapy, such as post-MI.

items.q: A patient is diagnosed with their first episode of acute pericarditis. What is the recommended duration of colchicine therapy to optimize long-term outcomes?
o: 12 months
1 month
6 months
3 months
items.exp: Colchicine administered for 3 months reduces the rate of recurrence in acute pericarditis.
r: Extended therapy beyond 6 months is not the standard recommendation for initial episodes.
Standard practice mandates a 3-month course to effectively reduce recurrence rates.
Six months of therapy is indicated only for recurrent cases, not the first episode.
Colchicine administered for 3 months reduces the rate of recurrence in acute pericarditis.
items.kp: Colchicine should be used for 3 months in initial pericarditis to halve recurrence.

items.q: A patient presents with hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and pulsus paradoxus. Echo confirms cardiac tamponade. Which intervention is contraindicated?
o: Monitoring hemodynamic status
Administration of furosemide
Urgent pericardiocentesis
Echo-guided drainage
items.exp: Diuretics are strictly avoided in cardiac tamponade to prevent worsening hypotension and decreased cardiac output.
r: Monitoring is necessary to assess the urgency and response to treatment in tamponade.
Diuretics are strictly avoided in cardiac tamponade to prevent worsening hypotension and decreased cardiac output.
Pericardiocentesis is the definitive and urgent treatment for cardiac tamponade.
Echo-guided pericardiocentesis is the standard and necessary approach for tamponade management.
items.kp: Manage tamponade with urgent pericardiocentesis; avoid diuretics and vasodilators which deplete preload.

items.q: A 32-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of sharp chest pain and pericardial friction rub, diagnosed as recurrent pericarditis. Which of the following is the most appropriate management strategy to prevent further recurrences?
o: Start long-term immunosuppression with azathioprine immediately upon diagnosis of recurrence.
Administer colchicine monotherapy for 3 months with abrupt cessation upon symptom resolution.
Restart aspirin or an NSAID combined with colchicine for at least 6 months, tapering based on CRP levels.
Initiate high-dose corticosteroids as the primary maintenance therapy for 6 months.
items.exp: Current guidelines mandate combination therapy and a gradual taper guided by inflammatory markers for at least 6 months.
r: Immunosuppression is reserved for refractory cases, not standard management for first recurrence.
Combination therapy with NSAIDs is required, and the minimum treatment duration is 6 months.
Current guidelines mandate combination therapy and a gradual taper guided by inflammatory markers for at least 6 months.
Corticosteroids are not first-line and increase the risk of recurrence when used early.
items.kp: Recurrent pericarditis management requires restarting NSAID/aspirin plus colchicine for at least 6 months with CRP-guided tapering.

items.q: A 45-year-old male with chronic kidney disease (CKD stage 4) presents with acute pericarditis. Which of the following modifications is necessary regarding his pharmacological management?
o: Initiate high-dose corticosteroid therapy instead of NSAIDs or colchicine.
Adjust the colchicine dosage and monitor for potential nephrotoxicity if using NSAIDs.
Avoid all anti-inflammatory treatments as they are strictly contraindicated in CKD.
Administer standard loading doses of colchicine to ensure rapid therapeutic effect.
items.exp: Dosage reduction is mandatory for colchicine in CKD, and NSAIDs pose specific risks for nephrotoxicity.
r: Corticosteroids remain second-line, and the primary issue is dose modification of conventional agents.
Dosage reduction is mandatory for colchicine in CKD, and NSAIDs pose specific risks for nephrotoxicity.
Management is possible with careful dosing adjustments and monitoring, not total avoidance.
Standard doses are unsafe; colchicine must be reduced in CKD patients.
items.kp: In CKD and elderly patients, colchicine requires dose reduction, and NSAIDs require careful monitoring for nephrotoxicity.

items.q: A 65-year-old male with gout is maintained on 0.6 mg colchicine daily. He is recently started on verapamil for supraventricular tachycardia. Which mechanism best explains the increased risk of colchicine toxicity in this patient?
o: Induction of P-glycoprotein transport pathways.
Reduced renal excretion via tubular secretion.
Inhibition of CYP3A4-mediated metabolism of colchicine.
Competitive binding to plasma albumin proteins.
items.exp: Verapamil inhibits CYP3A4, leading to decreased colchicine clearance and elevated systemic toxicity.
r: Verapamil acts as an inhibitor, not an inducer, of P-glycoprotein efflux transporters.
The interaction primarily involves metabolic pathways rather than competition for renal transport.
Verapamil inhibits CYP3A4, leading to decreased colchicine clearance and elevated systemic toxicity.
Colchicine toxicity in this interaction is driven by metabolic inhibition, not protein displacement.
items.kp: Strong CYP3A4 and P-gp inhibitors like verapamil and clarithromycin significantly increase colchicine plasma concentrations, necessitating dose reduction or avoidance.

items.q: A 45-year-old male presents with sharp, pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward. His ECG shows diffuse PR segment depression. Echocardiography is negative for effusion. Which of the following is sufficient to establish a definitive diagnosis of acute pericarditis in this patient?
o: Repeating the echocardiogram in 48 hours to look for effusion.
Testing for serum troponin levels to evaluate for myocarditis.
Ordering an urgent cardiac MRI for tissue characterization.
Presence of a pericardial friction rub on auscultation.
items.exp: Clinical diagnosis requires two of the four criteria; he has pain and PR depression, rub confirms etiology.
r: Current criteria are met by two features; waiting for a third is clinically unnecessary and delays diagnosis.
Troponins reflect myocardial involvement but do not meet the diagnostic criteria for acute pericarditis itself.
Diagnosis is primarily clinical; MRI is reserved for complicated cases or diagnostic uncertainty, not routine requirement.
Clinical diagnosis requires two of the four criteria; he has pain and PR depression, rub confirms etiology.
items.kp: Acute pericarditis diagnosis necessitates two of four criteria: characteristic pain, pericardial rub, ECG changes, or new/worsening pericardial effusion.
